what_its_for: Fluticasone is a steroid medicine that reduces swelling and irritation. Depending on the form you use, it can treat nasal allergy symptoms like stuffy or runny nose and sneezing (nasal spray), asthma and breathing problems (inhaler), or itchy, red, or inflamed skin conditions like eczema (cream or ointment). It does NOT work for sudden asthma attacks.
how_to_take: For nasal spray: Blow your nose gently first. Shake the bottle, tilt your head slightly forward, and spray into each nostril while breathing in slowly through your nose. Do not spray into the center wall of your nose. For inhaler: Breathe out fully, place the inhaler in your mouth, press down, and breathe in slowly and deeply. Hold your breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out. Always rinse your mouth with water and spit after using an inhaler to help prevent a mouth or throat infection. For skin cream or ointment: Apply a thin layer to the affected skin area only. Rub it in gently. Wash your hands before and after applying. Do not use on the face, underarms, or groin unless your doctor tells you to.
dosing: Your dose depends on which form of fluticasone you are using and what condition is being treated. A common adult dose for nasal spray is 1 to 2 sprays in each nostril once a day. For inhalers, the dose is usually 1 to 2 puffs once or twice a day. For skin cream, apply once or twice a day as directed. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed. Do not use more than directed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store fluticasone at room temperature, away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Keep nasal sprays and inhalers at room temperature — do not freeze them. Keep the cap on when not in use. Store skin creams and ointments tightly closed. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not use fluticasone more often or in larger amounts than your doctor prescribed. Avoid contact with your eyes — if the spray or cream gets in your eyes, rinse with water right away. Do not cover treated skin areas with tight bandages or plastic wrap unless your doctor tells you to. Tell your doctor if you have been around anyone who has chickenpox, measles, or tuberculosis (TB), as fluticasone can lower your ability to fight infections. Avoid stopping the inhaler or nasal spray suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if you notice: white patches or sores in your mouth or throat (possible yeast infection from inhaler use), vision changes or eye pain, worsening breathing problems, signs of infection such as fever, chills, or body aches, skin thinning, stretch marks, or unusual bruising near areas where cream was applied, swelling of the face or ankles, unusual weight gain, or if your symptoms do not improve after 1 to 2 weeks of regular use. Call 911 or go to the emergency room right away if you have a sudden severe asthma attack.
when_it_works: Fluticasone does not work right away. For nasal allergy symptoms, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of daily use before you feel the full benefit. For asthma inhalers, improvement in breathing may take several days to a few weeks. Skin creams may start to relieve itching and redness within a few days. It is important to keep using it every day as directed, even if you feel better.
special_populations: Children: Fluticasone can be used in children, but it may slow growth with long-term use. Your child's doctor will monitor their height regularly. Use the lowest effective dose. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before using fluticasone. It is generally considered low risk when used as directed, especially the nasal spray, but your doctor should know. Elderly: No special dose changes are usually needed, but older adults should be monitored for bone thinning (osteoporosis) with long-term use. People with liver problems: Use with caution — your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely.
